I was writing a statement of a formalization challenge for lean-eval when I realized mathlib doesn't have the Suzuki groups. I'm far from an expert in these but my understanding is that we normally parameterize the group family as Sz(q) for q = 2^(2*n + 1) and view them as subgroups of SL_4(F_q).

What is the right way to express a hypothesis on q in a definition? The most common hypothesis I've seen on a definition is an implicit argument that p is prime, but whereas that is common this is a one off. We could pass an explicit hypothesis that "there exists n such that" but it would make it totally unwieldy to refer to the groups. Another option might be the existence of such n an implicit hypothesis? There are other ways of defining the family which avoid those issues such as Suzuki(n) := Sz(2^(2*n+1)) for any natural n, but then it's breaking with the naming convention of a vast tome of literature?

Although I'd like to figure out a specific solution to this question, more generally how does mathlib handle definitions of families which are not well defined for certain values?

Ryan Smith said:

There are other ways of defining the family which avoid those issues such as Suzuki(n) := Sz(2^(2*n+1)) for any natural n, but then it's breaking with the naming convention of a vast tome of literature?

I would suggest parametrizing them on n instead of q. This is what is done for docs#GaloisField, for example.
Thanks, if that's how GF does it then we should probably do the same for the groups.

I know PRs are supposed to be fairly short when possible, but this may require some lemmas about generators and relations just to prove a first statement like "the order of Sz(n) is __". Is it a problem if a PR is basically just setup for later stuff and doesn't prove anything worthwhile on its own? Also, if there are lemmas which are just grinding a bit on something like generators would those be appropriately labeled protected?
I think that's normal. Also there's some PRs in flight about group presentation you should look at so you can build on top of instead of repeating work

Ryan Smith said:

Also, if there are lemmas which are just grinding a bit on something like generators would those be appropriately labeled protected?

protected may not be what you mean here, it just changes the namespace of a theorem. private actually hides it from being imported which I'm guessing is what you meant to ask about. I don't think it makes sense to mark them private, I think if you need this API then other people are likely to as well. One of the ideas is to not just prove your intended theorem but also build nice general API for the next person that may need to do something similar. (private is generally used when you are proving something that is not meant to be exposed or is just an intermediate step in a more powerful theorem that follows.)
